chunks.text: G'day. It's 1:00. Did the committee agree to come back at 1:00? Was that right, Todd? Oh, sorry. You're just on mute. Yes. No problem. Yeah. No problem. We were. And I'm sure with Jamie's fine chairing, are we up to the Lifewise Trust? We are. We're right on- Mate... on track.
I'll just leave you to it, Jamie. Okay, looks like we've got Carl. We'll just wait for Carlo and Rima to join us back. So far, so good, though? Great.

Hey, Rima. Hi, Habib. Hi, team. Hi, Mr. Chair. Just I was waiting to be let in. You're all good. Jamie did okay. He did all right. Humble man. Okay, we got Carl and Paulo, got Dan. We have a quorum, so I am happy for us to kick on and start our afternoon session with the Lifewise Trust with Pam and Anne-Marie, if they could be let in, please.

Hi, Pam. Hello. How are you? I'm very good, thank you. Just getting my camera off. Sorry. Yeah. That's okay. And do you have Anne-Marie joining you? Anne-Marie's here, too. Oh, there you both are. Fantastic. Lovely to see you both. Thank you for submitting to us. We have read your submission.

So you have 10 minutes. We would ask that you leave a couple of minutes at the end for questions any of the members may have. But completely over to you to begin your submission. Thank you. Thank you very much. E raeranga tere ma. Tena koutou, tena koutou, tena koutou katoa. Ko Wai au. My name's Pam Elgar, and I'm the CEO of Lifewise and Methodist Mission Northern.

Lifewise is a large social and community service organization in the Auckland and Rotorua regions. My background includes 20 years of governance in the not-for-profit NGO sector, as well as an executive career in both public sector banking and not-for-profit. And I'll hand you over to Anne-Marie. Kia ora, and thank you for this opportunity.

My name is Anne-Marie Sutcliffe. I'm a registered psychiatric nurse and general manager of community services for Lifewise and Methodist Mission Northern. I've got a 40-year history of working in mental health and community services, as well as working in the public service sector. My services at Lifewise and Methodist Mission Northern sit across a really broad and connected system for people and whanau, and those people and whanau are among some of the most vulnerable in our community.

I've got services that work in housing and homelessness responses and homelessness outreach and family and community services, early childhood education, and wellbeing support. We aim to support people with practical pathways back into connection, safety, and stability. And together, all of those services work as one system.

We go and we meet people where they are, we build trusted relationships over time, and we try and link people to the right support so that their immediate need, their long-term wellbeing, and wider community safety are addressed together. Yeah. So we don't intend to repeat the submission. You've got that. But essentially, we do want to urge the Select Committee not to support the Summary Offences Amendment Bill because in our view, it does criminalize rough sleeping and begging without addressing the root causes of homelessness, addiction, trauma,

poverty, or mental health need. In our experience, safer communities are created when people are supported into safe accommodation with effective wraparound services, not when they're displaced from public spaces or pushed into less visible and less safe places.

Existing legal powers already allow police, council, and business owners to respond to genuine harm, including breach of the peace, trespass, obstruction, disorderly behavior, and breaches of local bylaws. This bill, in our view, risks undermining years of trust-based, trauma-informed work between outreach teams, street whanau, businesses, police, council, and other community services, while increasing the pressure on the justice system and public services rather than delivering better outcomes at a lower cost.

If the bill proceeds, Lifewise strongly recommends that rough sleeping, intent to inhabit, and begging are removed as grounds for a move on order, and that police must first connect people with an accredited social service provider with additional safeguards for young people under 17 through whanau, legal guardians, or Oranga Tamariki.

So I want to just talk really briefly about a story from our outreach team, and this is really talking to the people aspects. This story's not unusual actually. It's painfully common. We met a person because they kept coming back to Merge, our community services cafe on Karanga-a-Hape Road. That person was sleeping rough.

They'd already been told to move on many, many times. More times than they can count, actually. They weren't asking for much from us. They wanted a coffee. They wanted somewhere warm. They wanted somewhere predictable, and somewhere where they could be seen without being judged. But over time with this person, as we got to know them, we learned that being moved on, to them, didn't feel neutral.

It felt absolutely frightening. They'd lived through trauma in their past life, and being approached by authority, being told to leave suddenly, and being treated as a problem when they were simply trying to survive sent them into a panic. So they moved, but they didn't move into housing. They moved into darker, more isolated places.

And it took weeks of consistent contact with us before they trusted us enough after that experience to talk about getting some support. And finally that happened, not because we pressured them or threatened them or demanded compliance, but because we stayed with them. Same people, time and time again, and we built a relationship, and they knew that we would still be there tomorrow.

And for us, this is what move on orders risk breaking. When people are forced to leave familiar places, they don't just disappear. They become harder to find, harder to help, more isolated, more afraid, and more at risk. And importantly, trust gets reset to zero.

So what eventually helped this person wasn't enforcement, it was relationship, dignity, being known by name, being met with patience instead of punishment. And that's why this proposed law worries us, both from a systemic approach, but also from an operational on the streets approach.

Every day we see safer communities are built by connection, not by exclusion, by housing people, supporting people, and staying with people long enough for trust to grow. For me, the key messages are clear. Move on orders don't solve homelessness. Housing and support solves homelessness, and trust is what makes that change possible.

So what we're asking the committee to be clear about is what is this bill trying to solve? What's the problem definition that we're trying to resolve? And then to be equally clear about what it will actually do. If a person is rough sleeping, has set up their belongings, or is sitting quietly with a sign asking for help, they're not creating homelessness.

They're showing us where homelessness already exists. Moving them on does not create a home, it doesn't create a health response, doesn't create an income or a safe place to sleep. It simply pushes people further from the relationships and services that can help, and it risks turning poverty, trauma, and survival into matters for police and the courts.

So our call to action is straightforward. Do not support this bill in its current form. At a minimum, remove rough sleeping, intent to inhabit, and begging as grounds for a move on order. Require police to connect people with accredited social services before any enforcement steps are taken, and require stronger safeguards in place for young people.

The committee has a choice here to endorse a response that displaces people, or to strengthen one that connects people to safety, dignity, and support. We urge you to choose the second path. Just in closing, as we mark Matariki, a time for reflection, renewal, and dreaming of what is possible, Lifewise exhorts the government and all political parties to work towards a more just future for everyone in Aotearoa, New Zealand.

That future must be shaped by systems, policies, and public services that uphold dignity, strengthen belonging, and create a genuinely human experience for all people, especially those that are most vulnerable and too often pushed to the margins. A just society for all is what we ask for.

We're very happy to answer any questions you might have. Thanks, Pam. Thank you Anne Marie. Really appreciate it. We've got two minutes left, so we've got a couple of people wanting to ask questions. We'll start with Camilla Belich. Thank you very much for your submission. It was a really good written submission and oral submission today. I was just really interested about the public nuisance bylaw that you mentioned in Auckland, and how you said that that was implemented in a way that was informed by a trauma informed approach, and I just wanted to know if you could explain to the

committee what that involves. In one minute. We're working with the compliance teams who enact the bylaws in Auckland City, and what that is is about how they engage with people who are rough sleeping. There's lots of different ways that you can engage with somebody who's terrified under a blanket of sleep. You can engage them in a way that doesn't build trust, or you can work with your outreach teams to actually engage them in a way that both deals with the behavior and the breaking of the bylaw, but also builds trust. So you can be pushed

awake by a foot, or you can be woken by somebody who crouches down and speaks to you gently. Yeah. And that's obviously the second approach is what we would-- and the bylaws give the possibility of doing that. There's nothing against that in the bylaws.

Thank you, and Dan Rosewarne. Thank you, Chair. So you highlighted that when people are moved on, they become harder to find and harder to help, and I'm keen to just quickly elaborate on that further. From the perspective of an outreach service, what impact would that have on your ability to connect people with housing, healthcare, addiction support, and those other services?

Yeah. Me? Yeah. So our experience is we work in the central Auckland area, along with Ka Hutia Kaha and Auckland City Mission. We know where people are, we know who people are, and we don't double up services. We're very careful about that, but we know where to go to engage with people.

When people are moved along, they're going to move out and out and out, and eventually we predict, in fact, we're almost seeing it already, that people are going to move to places where they're harder to be moved on. It's a frightening experience to be moved on by the police for people, anybody really, but particularly people with a trauma history.

What will happen, we predict, is that, in fact, we're already seeing it a little bit, is that people will move from where we find them, accessible and regular, to a stream, to a bush. We've heard of people going bush in Henderson, places like that, to places where it's much, much harder and less efficient pragmatically for our outreach services to find them.

Thank you. Thank you. And thank you, Pam and Anne-Marie. We really appreciate your time in coming to submit to us today, so thank you. No problem at all. All the best with your mahi. Thank you. Okay, we're now onto Extension Rebellion Ōtepoti, and we've got Jen Olsen.

Hey, Jen. Thank you for- Hey... joining us this afternoon. We can see you and hear you nice and clearly. Jen, you've got 10 minutes. We'd love it if you left a few minutes at the end for some of the members to ask questions if they have them. But over to you, Jen. Okay. Thank you. Kia ora koutou ko Jen Olsen toku ingoa. Thanks for the opportunity.

And, yeah, I'd really like to endorse the two previous speakers. I worked in social services for over 30 years, including as a mental health support worker and as a social worker. And I'm also a climate activist, and I see links between the social justice issues that are raised by this bill, the effects of colonization, and the climate and ecological emergency.

I'm opposed to this Summary Offences Bill. I see it as an attempt to conceal the consequences of the failure of our society to provide the basic necessities of life for everyone. And that failure is just one symptom of the failure of our economic system, which has not only failed to deliver homes for all our citizens, it's failed to honor Crown obligations to Māori, failed to reduce the emissions that are leading to catastrophic climate change, and it's failed to protect our environments from biodiversity loss and ecological breakdown.

But anyway, to return to the bill, my concerns include the vulnerability of youth, disregard for the principles of totality, and the callous attitude towards some of the least fortunate members of our society. The evidence from the University of Otago reports that nearly half of all homeless people in Aotearoa are aged under 25. Most are homeless due to circumstances outside of their control, such as family violence, poverty, and overcrowding.

And youth may not comply with move on orders simply because there is nowhere safe for them to go. Youth that have aged out of Oranga Tamariki care, two-thirds of whom are Māori, may have no whanau support, and the services for homeless youth are extremely limited. The Waitangi Tribunal in 2023 found that the Crown had breached the principles of equity and active protection in its lack of support for homeless rangatahi, and this bill compounds that breach.

Research has consistently also shown that contact with the justice system in adolescence leads to more frequent contact later in life. So this bill increases the long-term risk for homeless youth. Criminalizing people who are in public places for safety reasons or who are unable to comply with police due to mental distress or cognitive issues when there are simply not enough resources in the community to support them, it's unfair and it's wrong.

The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists, the Mental Health and Wellbeing Commission, and the Mental Health Foundation have all highlighted in recent years increasing levels of mental distress, particularly amongst young people, and that the mental health services in Aotearoa are not meeting those needs.

Nothing has substantially changed since 2023, when a report from 500 mental health physicians concluded that the mental health services in Aotearoa are not fit for purpose. So yeah, this is something I've witnessed at first hand, the lack of resources and the difficulty finding affordable and supported accommodation for people with mental illness or with learning disabilities. Workers in mental health do everything they can, but there's no substitute for comprehensive and properly resourced services. That's what we need.

Our services are fragmented. They are siloed due to moves to tighten eligibility criteria and funding over the years. No one has the responsibility to follow through with an individual and ensure that that person's needs are met. Radio New Zealand reported just the other day that each month for the past 16 months, there were 1,000 more inquiries to MSD about emergency housing than there were actual formal applications submitted.

That's 1,000 people out there needing help who didn't even get through to applying for it. And for those who did make it to a formal application and were declined, a third were offered nothing. Nothing at all. And these are issues well known to frontline workers like police.

Giving police powers to ask people to move on is just shifting the problem from one place to another. We have citizens of Aotearoa homeless and unwell in our streets. About a third of homeless people are Maori, tangata whenua of this land, suffering from the long-term effects of colonization, loss of land, livelihood, and community, and we are just telling them to go away. Brunis Hickey reported that this government is currently building more prison beds than beds in affordable homes.

That's a disgrace. It brings shame to this government and anyone who supports this heartless legislation. We know that there are not enough affordable homes in Aotearoa. It's the result of housing being used for many years as an investment and new kainga ora projects being stopped.

Over 3,000 planned new builds were stopped by this government. Public housing is not an optional extra for society. It's an essential service to provide all our citizens a life of dignity. Research evidence in Aotearoa shows unequivocally that the answer to homelessness is support into suitable housing.

Well, who knew? Aotearoa is a rich country, and the rich are becoming more and more wealthy. The collective wealth of the country's 150 richest individuals and families has grown, this is mind-boggling, by $26.9 billion in one year. This is obscene when people are homeless and begging on the streets.

Poverty is increasing. The New Zealand Council of Christian Social Services has shown that there are 473,000 people in Aotearoa right now experiencing material hardship. Poverty is the result of deliberate policies that have increased the gap between rich and poor, such as maintaining levels of unemployment as a strategy to reduce inflation, encouraging the use of housing as an investment, and allowing virtual monopolies on food supplies, privatizing services, user pays.

The list goes on. And now this government wants to hide the results by moving people who demonstrate the failure of their policies out of sight so we don't have to look at the human cost. What is the economy for if it is not to provide for the people of Aotearoa, to provide the necessities of life, shelter being the very first? An economy that fails to do that is a failure, no matter what the books say.

So we see the parallel consequences resulting from government policies focusing on a narrow view of economy and growth. We see increased poverty and social injustice alongside increasing wealth and the influence of an elite few. We have blatant breaches of good faith surrounding Te Tiriti o Waitangi alongside claims of equality in society, and we have increasing climate-related emergencies and threatened extinctions of our endemic wildlife alongside a disregard for emissions reduction, plans to enable more extractive industries, and treatment of the environment as a

disposable resource. We're in the midst of a polycrisis that's not only a social crisis like the one of homelessness and poverty, but an environmental one of rising temperatures and unstable weather events, and an international political crisis of wars, resource scarcity, and displaced people.

Aotearoa cannot separate itself from the rest of the world in this and can't deny that our social problems and our environmental problems are linked by our political attitude. The same short-term policies of exploitation and prioritization of financial gain have resulted in the social injustices we see in colonization, homelessness, and the climate and ecological emergency we are all facing.

This legislation is in the same spirit as climate denial, and I'm asking you now, reject this bill in its entirety. Thank you. Thanks, Jen, and thank you for your oral submission. We have time for one question if anybody would be interested to ask. That's quite all right. It's not a reflection on your submission, Jen.

We have- No, I didn't expect any questions. It's pretty clear-cut really, isn't it? We thank you for your time, Jen. Thanks for coming in. You're very welcome. Thanks for listening. Okay. Bye. All right. We're now going to have Pamela Greeley coming on, so we'll just wait for her to come online.

Hey, Pamela. Thank you for joining us today. We have read your submission. You've got five minutes, and if you'd like to leave a little bit of time at the end for questions, we would welcome that. But over to you. Kia ora koutou. Ko Pamela Grilli toku ingoa. Thank you for the opportunity to speak. I do want to start by acknowledging that businesses, retailers, and members of the public do sometimes experience intimidating or disruptive behavior in public places.

Those concerns are real, and they do deserve to be taken seriously. However, I don't believe this bill addresses the cause of those problems. It simply addresses their visibility. The bill mistakes homelessness for the problem. Rough sleeping and begging are usually symptoms of housing insecurity, trauma, mental illness, addiction or poverty, or other circumstances. Moving someone from one street to another doesn't solve any of these things. It simply relocates the problem.

I live in the beautiful Coromandel, and we are seeing people, either of their own volition because they're already being moved on, we're seeing more and more homelessness in Coromandel, and we don't have the infrastructure to deal with them. We have very small community services who are, again, being pulled apart by these because they just don't have the resources to deal with them.

Sorry, lost my place here. My own experience has been that people sleeping rough often want something very simple. They want to just be treated like people. I always acknowledge them if they're asking for food or money, and I'm in a position to help with whatever their request is, I will. But I've found that simply acknowledging them, saying hello, and recognizing their humanity is just as important.

This bill treats people experiencing homelessness primarily as a public order problem. I believe we should first recognize them as members of our community who deserve dignity and support. And finally, I find it difficult to reconcile this bill with the government's focus on reducing public spending. During COVID, we demonstrated that providing emergency accommodation significantly reduced rough sleeping. If we reduce housing support, move people on, and then imprison them for breaching a move on order, we are choosing one of the

most expensive responses available. Housing people costs money. Imprisoning them costs considerably more. I believe New Zealand can do better than moving vulnerable people from place to place. We should be investing in solutions that help people regain stability rather than criminalizing them for being homeless.

I only had a tube of wine gums for lunch, sorry. Before I finish, I'd ask the committee to remember that the people affected by this bill are not strangers. They are our neighbors, our workmates, our friends, our rangatahi, and sometimes our whānau. Many New Zealanders are only a few setbacks away from housing insecurity. A lost job, an illness, a relationship breakdown, or an unexpected expense can change someone's circumstances remarkably quickly.

I hope any response to homelessness reflects that shared humanity and focuses on helping people regain stability rather than simply moving them on. Thank you. Thank you, Pamela. I will just see if there are-- Yeah, there are a couple of members with questions. We've got time for both of them, so we'll start with Camilla Belich.

I'll let Lawrence go first because I've had a few first questions. Dr Lawrence Yun. Cool. Thank you so much, Chair. Thank you for that submission, Pamela. I think my question, and something that we've been asking for a little while, which is in your area, particularly in Coromandel, being more rural and regional, the experience might be different.

If people are moved on, would you know where would they be moving to? And for example, then what sort of services would they likely then have or not have because they've been moved on? So they don't have their whānau support. We have a number of 501s.

We have a number of people with mental illnesses that we know in town. We know who they are. They spend a lot of time moving between different rohe. I often pick them up hitchhiking because they've decided they're going to go somewhere else. We don't have enough emergency housing. Emergency housing is really hard to come by in Coromandel.

We're 50% holiday homes. There are not a lot of free houses. So basically, we're trying to help the people that we know because they are part of our community. And we know when they disappear for a few days, they've just relocated themselves. You see them standing on the side of State Highway 25 with their thumbs out.

So it's a real challenge for us as much as it is for people in the cities and the towns. Thank you. Right. And Camilla? Thanks. Just a question. Thanks for your well-written submission. I really like the bit where you talked about how people don't realize sometimes how close people are to homelessness.

Mm-hmm. And I don't think we've focused on this in question so much, but that's reflected in some of the submissions, I think, that described homelessness as a domino. And so I just wanted to give you the opportunity to expand on that. I think sometimes there's this tendency to other homelessness, but actually it may affect more people in our community than we realize. So I just wanted to see if you wanted to expand on that.

Yeah. Again, we see that we're also very poorly served for regular full-time work in rural areas a lot of the time. People are surviving on next to nothing. When benefits are cut, when they can't afford to put petrol in their cars, when all of these things happen, they lose their jobs. And then again, they lose their homes because there's no other way for them to get any money other than by a benefit, and they can't get to their benefit appointments because there's nothing locally. They have to go to the nearest town, which is about an hour away, no public transport.

So we can see how that's all happening. Like you say, it's a domino. The domino effect is real, and it's closer than you think. Great. Thank you, Pamela. Really appreciate you writing both a written submission and presenting to us today. So thank you very much for your time, and enjoy the beautiful Coromandel as well.
Thank you. Great. Okay. We have got Sheree, who's now going to be presenting to us.

Oh, okay. I can see Matthew. Ah, we don't have Sheree yet. Okay. We will carry on, and we will go to Matthew instead. Hey, Matthew. Thank you for joining us. Appreciate you being here. You got five minutes. We've read your submission, but please do leave time at the end for some questions as well. But totally over to you. Okay. Thank you, everyone. Look, I want to start off by thanking the select committee for allowing me to submit on this bill, and congratulations also to you, Mr. Chair, for your recent promotion. So my name is Matthew De Rossini.

I'm a local student here in Ōtautahi, and I organized the opposition to the Move On orders, bill when it was first announced. So I had the great privilege of hosting a rally and a space to support and amplify the voices of our homeless community here at Christchurch. And it was those voices that inform my submission today. So I've been listening to the submissions this morning.

I've heard overwhelmingly, as I hope the committee has as well, that there is not a good amount of support for this bill from the New Zealand public. I want to talk with the submission of Terangi Cleaver when she asked, "Move on where? Where are these move on orders supposed to apply to?" I also want to talk with the submission of Sharon Halborn, who spoke of the importance of love and compassion when solving the issues we have in society.

In my written submission, I did recommend that a nonpartisan approach should be taken to address issues such as homelessness. And so it is really sad to see certain members of this committee using submissions as an excuse to launch attacks on the opposition. I want to start my own submission by saying that I want to see a New Zealand where every single person has safety and dignity in what they need to thrive, and that does include us business owners as well.

And that's precisely why I don't support this bill. This bill touches upon a complex issue that is a result of systematic failures. All evidence points to the fact that this bill will not solve an issue, but will instead displace it. And I think of the gentleman living rough on the streets of my suburb in Riccarton. He moved away from the city center because police have already begun moving on homeless people from the city center.

This bill will isolate people. Here in Christchurch, we have the red zone, which is the block of land abandoned after the white earthquake. It's a dangerous piece of land with roaming dogs and live electricity, as well as a complete isolation from the support services that many people rely on. Despite this, there is already an established homeless community in the red zone, and it's a community that is struggling.

They are sick, they are cold, and they go about. This bill will push more people to the red zone, and it will kill people. I do not want this bill to proceed in any form, but in light of the government's insistence to continue with it, I do want the select committee to seriously consider whether applying bill to rough sleeping and begging is the best course of action. We know that these sections make the bill inconsistent with the Bill of Rights Act. Official advice has consistently urged the government to drop these parts of the bill.

If this bill does continue unamended, it will paint an incredibly sad portrait of our nation. I grew up in a country where we cared for people, and I don't know where that's gone. That's all I have to say to the committee. I'm happy to take any questions. Thank you very much. Thank you, Matthew, and thank you for your very well-considered submission. Really appreciate it. I've got a question from Rima Naklay.

Kia ora, Matthew. Thanks for your submission and for caring. Hey, look, you started off by saying that this bill doesn't do anything to solve homelessness. On what basis do you feel that this bill is meant to solve homelessness? Where'd you get that understanding from, Matthew?

No, so this bill, I don't believe that this bill is intended to solve homelessness. I think ultimately we have an issue in this country. It's an issue that's at its highest reported level according to many community providers. We need to be addressing this issue, and the proposals that are being brought about by this government at the moment, such as this bill, for the most part, do not address the issues that we're seeing in our country.

Okay. I'll let Camilla. I had another question, but all good. Thanks, Matthew. Camilla. Thanks. Thanks for your submission, and for the work that you've been doing on this bill. The question I had, you mentioned homelessness and rough sleeping, but another area which has come up a wee bit in the submissions on this bill and in the commentary has been the impact on young people 14 to 18. Did you have, and sorry if I missed it in your written submission, any comment to make on the inclusion of that group?

Yeah. Well, a lot of the people I see on the streets of Ōtautahi are young people. And I just cannot understand why this bill applies to 14-year-olds. I think these are people who are so vulnerable. We need to be supporting them. We need to be providing them with adequate social services and wraparound support, and this bill just does not address that at all.

Thanks, Matthew. Thank you very much for both your written and your oral submission and coming before us today. Really appreciate it. So thank you. Kia ora. Thank you. All right. Members, we've got Sheree Fluntoff now, so we'll just have Sheree promoted.

Hey, Sheree. Thank you for joining us today. There you are. We can see you. You're on mute, but thank you very much for coming before us. We have read your submission. You have five minutes, so please do leave a little bit of time at the end, and we may ask you some questions, but in your hands. Thank you, Tom, and hello, members of the committee.

I've come on not as an expert in the area of homelessness, but as someone who does understand how policy can and should work, and also someone who has strong feelings on how we should treat those that are most vulnerable. Because we're not a country that believes in kicking people when they are down.

There are penalties already for illegal behavior. We do not need to criminalize being homeless, which is in itself an incredibly vulnerable position to be in. And there's so many things that can cause homelessness, whether it's mental health, relationship breakdowns, death of a loved one, ill health. There's just so many different things that people are already dealing with.

I personally would not want to be sleeping out in the cold, even in Tauranga, which does have quite a mild climate. I feel so sorry for the people that do have to deal with that already, and do not believe that we should be making that a crime. I also do feel for the shopkeepers who find it challenging to have homeless people outside their shops.

And I think the only reasonable response to that would be to give people somewhere better to go. So instead of criminalizing finding somewhere warm and sheltered to hang out in bad or even good weather, we should be looking at how we can give them somewhere better to go. And if we are really sensible about it and want to use our resources wisely, making sure that we're giving them some of those social supports like mental health treatment, somewhere to live, good food to eat, and the opportunity to get themselves into a place where they can actually sustain

paying their own way, getting a job, contributing to the society more, rather than just criminalizing them and giving ourselves more ongoing costs in the process of doing so for housing them in prisons instead of working towards them being productive members of society. So yeah, if we're going to have a bill about homelessness, it should be about making sure that we're putting those supports in place to reduce the problem and to give them somewhere else to go, because they're not going to hang around in shop doorways if

there's somewhere better for them, are they? Anyway, that's pretty much the point I wish to make. Just to add that voice so that you know how many people out here in the country are concerned that we don't want to kick those that are most vulnerable when they're already down. So yeah.

Thank you, Sheree. Thank you, and good to see another Tauranga local. So, got a question from Dr. Lawrence Sun Han. Cool. Thank you, Chair. Thank you Sheree, for your submission. I think one of the things the committee has heard today is around the balance between safety and wellbeing of homeless whanau, but as far as ensuring that business owners and customers are safe as well, when you do see aggressive behavior.

Can I check, do you think when businesses are raising concerns around potentially behavior issues or even rough sleeping or homelessness, that their intention is for them to be incarcerated and criminalized, as opposed to finding accommodations or finding the wraparound support that they actually need?

I think there's a couple of different questions within that. Mm. So, aggressive behavior can be addressed with existing laws. It's a separate issue altogether. Getting them to move on, I think a lot of the business owners just want them to be somewhere else.

The problem with this bill is that it is very much criminalizing a state of being rather than criminalizing a behavior, and it's not about actually investing in getting people alternatives. So helping them want to be somewhere else, helping them have the skills and the backstops of housing and mental health support and other things that they might need to be able to be somewhere else.

So yeah, this bill very much is just about the rough sleeping, not about the aggressive behaviors.
